messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos is a 64-year-old jeweler, divorced for over a decade, who sought treatment for what he described as a lifetime of “waiting for the other shoe to drop.” He grew up in a small apartment in San Antonio, where his father’s violent rages were a fixture of his early years. He still sees those nights in snapshot images: the flash of a ceramic lamp shattering against the wall, the silver glint of a letter opener his father once snatched from the kitchen drawer, his mother’s voice rising until it cracked. Each memory is vivid and detailed, as if frozen in amber, and when it surfaces he is flooded with guilt—guilt that he did nothing, guilt that he survived unscathed while his mother bore the bruises. These memories are not just painful; they are instructions. Whenever they come, Carlos begins to monitor his own thoughts obsessively, scanning for any hint of the same violent potential he fears lives inside him. He also tries to suppress the images entirely, pushing them down with work or silence, but the effort leaves him drained and more convinced that he is weak. The suppression itself kept his mind on edge, and ordinary moments—a customer walking in, a phone ringing—began to feel like potential flashpoints, turning his daily work into a cascade of triggers he could no longer ignore.

For decades, Carlos managed by staying busy. As a jeweler, he spent long hours alone at his bench, repairing watches and setting stones—work that demanded intense focus and kept his hands occupied. But his daily environment has become a minefield. A customer raising his voice over a repair bill triggers a cascade: Carlos’s eyes flick to the glass cases, then to the small hammer on his bench, calculating whether it could be used as a weapon. He watches every male customer with hypervigilance, reading body language for signs of aggression. Shouting, male presence, and direct confrontations have become unbearable. He has come to believe that if he relaxes—even for a moment—something terrible will happen, so he avoids any quiet pause, filling every second with motion or thought. Because he never stayed still long enough to discover that the danger might not arrive, his body remained locked in a state of high alert, the sense of threat as vivid and urgent as if the event were still happening. This constant threat monitoring only reinforces his negative appraisals: he has failed in his most important role as a man and protector, he is weak for being so afraid, and he has lost his connection to the close-knit Latin American community he once valued, because he cannot bear the noise and unpredictability of family gatherings.

The causal cycles are relentless. A memory of his father’s face tightening before a blow will make Carlos glance around his workshop, noticing the metal shears, the small torch, the heavy ring mandrel—all potential weapons. That threat appraisal then sends him back to the memory with fresh guilt, confirming that he is still the frightened boy who could not act. When a confrontation does occur, even a minor disagreement with a colleague, Carlos feels his negative self-beliefs solidify: he should have been stronger, he should have stopped it, he is a failure. These beliefs, in turn, make him more sensitive to any raised voice or male presence, so he starts scanning exits before the argument is over. His maladaptive strategies—suppressing thoughts, monitoring for signs of craziness, refusing to let down his guard—paradoxically make the memories more intrusive, because the effort of suppression keeps the trauma front and center. And every time he suppresses, he reinforces the idea that the memories are too dangerous to face, which deepens his sense of weakness and isolation.

Carlos finally came to therapy because the avoidance is no longer working. A few weeks ago, a new client—a large, loud man—shouted about a repair delay, and Carlos felt his chest tighten so severely that he excused himself and locked himself in the bathroom, trembling. That evening, alone in his apartment, he realized he had not spoken to his sister in three months, had not attended a single family party in over a year, and could no longer trust his own perception of safety. He is terrified that he is losing his mind, but he is also desperate to stop the loop. What he most hopes for is to feel the ground beneath his feet again—to sit quietly in a room with another man and not watch the shadows.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not contain a paragraph where the sense of threat directly causes the perception of triggers or makes ordinary stimuli more triggering.
